transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tomás (Redwood SE), Ravi (Elysian Head of ML), Lena (Platform Eng), Marco (SRE)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round of intros then Tomás will walk through the prefetch playbook we shared.
[00:22] Ravi (Elysian): hey, hi, thanks. we've been running a small proof with a cached prefix layer but hit rates have been poor during peak windows, and tail latency spikes.
[00:35] Tomás (Redwood SE): cool, let's dig in. quick note - i'll reference the playbook link: https://redwood.example.com/prefetch-playbook - i'll also show a couple sims. bear with me, my screen share has a slight lag.
[01:05] Tomás (Redwood SE): first principle, prefetching is about shifting predictable token work off the critical path. we recommend a 2-tier approach: deterministic prefix caching for known templated prompts + probabilistic prefetch for long-tail prompts.
[01:36] Lena (Elysian): by deterministic you mean a hash on the fixed prompt header? our prompts have per-user personalization so not always exactly the same.
[01:48] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, deterministic keys are usually normalized prompt headers + schema fields. for personalization we strip nonessential ephemeral tokens then build a prefix-signature. we use a stable digest - murmur or xxhash works fine - avoiding full prompt as key. note: imperfect transcription - i typed mu-mer earlier in notes, it's murmur.
[02:20] Marco (SRE): are we talking about KV cache or an LRU in front of the model? how does this persist in our VPC pilot?
[02:33] Tomás (Redwood SE): good question. the approach we propose is a hybrid: an in-memory KV for hot KV cache at inference nodes + optional persistent prefix-store in your VPC (redis or RocksDB) for warm items. the runtime will consult in-node KV, if miss then local prefetch worker can prime the model's KV cache asynchronously.
[02:58] Ravi (Elysian): what hit rates should we expect? our workload is conversational and has many short unique prompts.
[03:12] Tomás (Redwood SE): depends on your entropy. with normalization + templating we typically see 20-45% effective token-level hit rate improvements for SaaS conversational workloads; if you can standardize a small set of system messages and few-shot examples the upper bound grows. i want to emphasize token-level vs request-level hit rates - they differ.
[03:45] Maya (Redwood AE): quick interjection - customers often confuse request cache hits with effective token compute saved. the playbook spells that out in section 2.
[04:00] Lena (Platform Eng): we care about tail p95/p99 latency. does prefetching increase load unpredictably? we saw spikes when many workers tried to prime the same prefix.
[04:15] Tomás (Redwood SE): yep that's a known thundering herd risk. mitigation patterns: single-flight prefetch (leader election per prefix), jittered backoff, and batching prefetches by affinity windows. also we recommend per-tenant rate limiting on background prefetch to avoid cross-tenant amplification.
[04:44] Marco (SRE): how do you guard against cache poisoning or leakage between tenants? our compliance team is strict.
[04:53] Tomás (Redwood SE): multi-tenant safety is top of mind. key rules: include tenant id in key namespace (never rely on implicit ingress isolation), encrypt at rest for persistent stores, and zero-copy isolation in runtime: per-tenant KV shards with eviction fences. for shared caches add tags and strict LRU windows per tenant plus quota tokens.
[05:20] Ravi (Elysian): eviction fences? can you unpack that?
[05:27] Tomás (Redwood SE): eviction fence is a lightweight guard - when we evict a prefix we write a tombstone with a short TTL so concurrent workers know not to re-prime that hotset immediately; helps avoid storms if a tenant suddenly invalidates many prefixes.
[05:54] Lena (Platform Eng): interesting. does the runtime support fine-grained shard placement? we have multiple AZs and sometimes keep tenants pinned to a subset for compliance.
[06:06] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, runtime supports shard hints. you can pin shard ranges to AZs and the smart router will prefer local shards, fallback to cross-AZ only if allowed. note that cross-AZ prefetch will add extra latency for cache fills.
[06:32] Maya (Redwood AE): wanted to flag quantization concern - a few customers saw slightly different tokenization leading to mismatched KV caches after quantizing models. Tomás, any notes?
[06:46] Tomás (Redwood SE): quantization can change model logits slightly and therefore cached KV validity. we recommend: run a deterministic eval of cache-consistency post-quant; use model-variant specific cache keys (include model checksum + quantization profile id in key namespace). that way cached prefixes from float32 model aren't wrongly used by int8 variant.
[07:20] Ravi (Elysian): that makes sense. for on-prem pilot we have an HSM-backed KMS for keys - does Redwood support integrating with customer KMS?
[07:33] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for encryption keys; note that cross-node key operations can add latency - we typically use local node key wrapping and central KMS for rotation only. we'll document specifics in the playbook.
[07:58] Marco (SRE): what's the storage footprint? if we persist warm prefixes for 100M requests per day, how big will the store grow?
[08:12] Tomás (Redwood SE): depends on prefix size and compression. typical prefix-store for conversational templates is 50-200 bytes per prefix key and 1-3KB per cache entry after kv-compressed weights; for 100M unique prefixes that's obviously huge. so strategy: TTL-based tiering, hotset-only persistence and bloom filters to avoid priming for very low frequency keys.
[08:47] Lena (Platform Eng): can we tune TTL per tenant? some tenants are high churn, others stable.
[08:54] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, TTL and eviction policy are configurable per-tenant and per-prefix-class. we support heuristics that adapt based on observed re-hit probability.
[09:12] Ravi (Elysian): about batching - we already batch request-level tokens on the server. does prefetching change batching behavior?
[09:23] Tomás (Redwood SE): prefetching can reduce batch sizes because you consume fewer tokens on the critical path, but we've implemented continuous batching so the runtime will still pack open requests. tradeoff: too aggressive prefetch can starve batch consolidation; recommended setting is conservative prefetch window that only primes prefixes predicted to be used within X ms.
[09:56] Maya (Redwood AE): question from procurement - is there a risk this increases cost due to unnecessary priming?
[10:05] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes if misconfigured. cost controls: budgeted prefetch quotas per tenant, costing by prefetch token counts, and instrumentation dashboards. the Optimize module can simulate savings vs priming overhead.
[10:28] Lena (Platform Eng): you mentioned bloom filters - are those per-tenant? false positives could waste priming.
[10:37] Tomás (Redwood SE): we usually have a global bloom filter for very low-latency checks plus per-tenant filters for mid-frequency items; false positive rates are tunable, and we use a probabilistic re-check if the bloom says present but in-node kv misses - then we probe persistent store.
[11:05] Marco (SRE): in the VPC pilot, can we keep the persistent prefix store on our infra (RDS/redis) or must it be managed by Redwood?
[11:16] Tomás (Redwood SE): in Private mode you manage the persistent store; Redwood operators can optionally manage it in Dedicated offering. for your on-prem we recommend local RocksDB with a small redis fronting layer. there's a docs snippet in the playbook.
[11:38] Ravi (Elysian): any real-world numbers on p99 improvement?
[11:45] Tomás (Redwood SE): in customer X we saw p99 drop from ~1.6s to ~800ms with a hybrid prefetch and KV strategy for a templated workflow. for high-entropy chat apps it's more modest, p99 from 1.2s to 900ms. i can share the benchmark spreadsheet.
[12:12] Maya (Redwood AE): can you share the micro-benchmark plan you'll run in the pilot?
[12:18] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, plan will include: synthetic hotset replay, randomized personalization token injection, cross-tenant storm test, quantized vs float parity check and persistent store failover scenarios.
[12:40] Lena (Platform Eng): about cache keys - how do we prevent collisions across tenants and model versions?
[12:48] Tomás (Redwood SE): key schema recommendation: {tenant_id}:{model_checksum}:{quant_profile}:{prefix_signature}. keep components short but collision-resistant. avoid naive truncation of hashes.
[13:10] Ravi (Elysian): do you ever use partial-key matching? like prefix grouping where similar prompts map to same cache key?
[13:21] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes that's the probabilistic grouping i mentioned earlier. we create canonical forms and equivalence buckets for paraphrases using small LSH or semantic hashing where appropriate. it's more compute upfront but improves hit density on long-tail. careful with privacy implications - we never store PII-derived buckets.
[13:50] Marco (SRE): heatmap visualization - will Redwood ship logs that show per-prefix hit-rate over time? our ops need that.
[13:59] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes, Console exposes per-prefix hotset dashboards, ability to drill into tenant shards, and anomaly alerts (sudden drop in prefix hit-rate). we can export CSVs for your SIEM.
[14:20] Maya (Redwood AE): side note - a few customers that used Anthropic reported different tokenization behaviors; that was called out by procurement as a vendor-risk. hence why checksum + model-id in keys is important.
[14:36] Ravi (Elysian): we have a question from our ML team: how to measure effective saved tokens from cache? is there a standard formula?
[14:46] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes: saved_tokens = sum_over_requests(prefix_hit_token_count * request_weight). rearranged it's measured by instrumenting runtime counters: token_attempted, token_served_from_cache, token_generated_by-model. we'll send an instrumentation snippet.
[15:12] Lena (Platform Eng): pilot timeline - do you recommend starting in Hosted then move to Private? we want to test on real traffic but maintain security posture.
[15:24] Tomás (Redwood SE): common pattern: stage 1 hosted sandbox against replayed production traffic, stage 2 dedicated with VPC peering for pilot, stage 3 Private on-prem for regulated tenants. since you have HSM and strict egress rules i'd suggest skipping broad hosted ingress and start with dedicated/VPC.
[15:50] Marco (SRE): if we run on-prem, are there additional operational burdens? e.g., telemetry, tracing?
[15:58] Tomás (Redwood SE): some telemetry requires access to the control plane; we provide an agent that scrubs PII and ships metrics to your SIEM; full debug traces can be kept inside your VPC per policy.
[16:20] Ravi (Elysian): procurement question again - cost model for prefetching versus saved tokens. will you provide a spreadsheet?
[16:29] Maya (Redwood AE): yes i'll attach the cost model spreadsheet and an example runbook after the call.
[16:36] Tomás (Redwood SE): one more technical caveat - for quantized models, some KV layers may benefit from re-computing certain attention caches deterministically. we have an option in runtime to fall back to compute-heavy but safe path when mismatch probability is above threshold.
[17:00] Lena (Platform Eng): can that be toggled per-tenant?
[17:05] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes per-tenant config via Console or API.
[17:18] Ravi (Elysian): ok, hypothetical: if tenant A invalidates a system prompt across all their users, how do you avoid each worker refilling simultaneously?
[17:28] Tomás (Redwood SE): that's single-flight + tombstone pattern; we also recommend rate-limited background re-prime with exponential backoff and central coordination via worker lease so only N workers will attempt re-prime.
[17:58] Marco (SRE): what's the recommended size for in-node KV? our nodes have 32GB of RAM reserved for inference; we can't allocate too much to cache.
[18:09] Tomás (Redwood SE): typical in-node KV is 10-30% of node RAM depending on model size and request concurrency. smaller KV with higher eviction aggressiveness plus persistent warm store is common. we'll run sizing sims during the pilot.
[18:33] Maya (Redwood AE): quick poll - does Elysian want Redwood to provision persistent store or manage it yourselves?
[18:41] Ravi (Elysian): we prefer manage in our VPC for compliance; may ask Redwood to help with ops runbook though.
[18:51] Maya (Redwood AE): noted.
[19:00] Tomás (Redwood SE): ops note - when you manage store, also ensure snapshot schedules and cold-start restore windows are understood; big warmstore restores can cause long tail during restarts. we advise gradual restore and prioritized hotset first.
[19:28] Lena (Platform Eng): any gotchas with TLS termination and persistent store encryption?
[19:34] Tomás (Redwood SE): ensure mutual TLS and service-to-service auth; for RocksDB local stores enable platform-level encryption and use KMS-wrapped keys. we'll provide a sample terraform module.
[19:55] Ravi (Elysian): could you summarize recommended initial config for pilot?
[20:00] Tomás (Redwood SE): sure - start with: small in-node KV (10GB), persistent RocksDB on HV with 7-day hot TTL, single-flight prefetch leader per prefix, include tenant_id+model_checksum in key schema, enable bloom filters for cold checks, set prefetch budget to 5% of normal compute. we'll put exact numbers in the playbook.
[20:30] Maya (Redwood AE): time check - we have ~40 mins left; want to tackle cross-tenant safety tests and a quick demo of the leader election logs.
[20:42] Tomás (Redwood SE): demo - i'll show log tail and leader lease behavior. apologies for slight audio fuzz.
[21:10] [DEMO - log tailing with leader leases and prefetch metrics - ~8 minutes audio, few silent pauses and typing sounds]
[29:40] Tomás (Redwood SE): demo notes: you can see lease grants for prefix XYZ, worker id 0x12 became leader and primed KV; subsequent requests hit in-node KV at 92% for that prefix during the window.
[30:05] Marco (SRE): that 92% seems high - what was the synthetic hotset size?
[30:12] Tomás (Redwood SE): that was a narrow synthetic hotset of top-500 prefixes. in realistic long-tail traffic it will be lower.
[30:30] Ravi (Elysian): would you recommend precomputing for some tenants offline? we have nightly batch jobs that could preprime common prefixes.
[30:41] Tomás (Redwood SE): absolutely - offline priming is low-cost for stable templates; combine with checksums to avoid redundant priming if content hasn't changed.
[31:00] Lena (Platform Eng): about privacy - if offline priming uses customer data do we need to mask?
[31:07] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes definitely mask PII and avoid storing direct user identifiers in prefix keys. use salted non-reversible mapping for any necessary mapping.
[31:28] Maya (Redwood AE): just flagging time. last 15 mins we'll do failure-mode scenarios and wrap with next steps.
[31:35] Tomás (Redwood SE): failure mode 1: persistent store unavailable - runtime shifts to in-memory only and increases miss-rate; mitigation: reduce prefetch budget and enable degraded mode. failure mode 2: KV checksum mismatch - fallback to compute-heavy deterministic path and emit alert. failure mode 3: tenant surge - enforce tenant-level throttles and prefetch quotas.
[32:20] Marco (SRE): in degraded mode do you queue requests or fail fast?
[32:26] Tomás (Redwood SE): we prefer graceful degradation: allow compute path for requests but disable background prefetch, and have a fast fail path for non-essential low-priority jobs.
[32:45] Ravi (Elysian): are there proven heuristics to pick prefetch budget?
[32:52] Tomás (Redwood SE): start with 2-5% of inferred token budget, monitor ROI (saved_tokens vs primed_tokens) and adapt. Optimize module can automatedly suggest adjustments after 48-72 hours.
[33:18] Lena (Platform Eng): fine-grained RBAC - can we restrict who can change prefetch budgets?
[33:24] Tomás (Redwood SE): Console supports RBAC and audit logs; we also integrate with SAML SSO for entitlement sync.
[33:40] Maya (Redwood AE): let's go through quick Q&A from procurement/infosec checklist.
[33:46] Ravi (Elysian): 1) SOC2/ISO documents? 2) encryption at-rest and in-transit? 3) data residency? 4) audit logs?
[33:56] Maya (Redwood AE): yes to all - we'll attach SOC2 report, details on KMS integration, and how audit logs are retained in your VPC.
[34:10] Marco (SRE): for the on-prem agent, are upgrades rolling? do they require restarts of inference nodes?
[34:17] Tomás (Redwood SE): upgrades are rolling and we support drain/rehydrate patterns to avoid cold starts; some kernel-level changes may require node restarts but those are planned during maintenance windows.
[34:38] [short pause, typing]
[34:52] Ravi (Elysian): high-level acceptability: we want predictable p99 under 1s for tier-1 tenants. think the hybrid approach can hit that with proper templating.
[35:05] Tomás (Redwood SE): yes that's achievable if you reduce prefix entropy for tier-1 flows and reserve dedicated capacity; we'll simulate in the benchmark.
[35:28] Maya (Redwood AE): last section: paperwork - we'll send pilot SOW and security addendum.
[35:35] Ravi (Elysian): please do.
[35:40] Maya (Redwood AE): thanks all — wrap up and recap next steps.
[35:46] [Meeting ends with small chitchat about weekend plans, background noise, and sign-offs]

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-heard acronyms (mu-mer -> murmur), and minor speaker attribution errors typical of automated transcript. Demo logs and benchmark sheets referenced: https://redwood.example.com/prefetch-playbook and https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/elysian-sim.csv
